articles.title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI agent & application、Startup & business
articles.summary: The startup allows software engineers to deploy teams of agents to work on various aspects of a project simultaneously.
articles.full_text:
Meta has acquired Conductor , an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.

The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog. “I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.” On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.

Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.

Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer.

The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert.

The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.

Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have.

The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.

Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up.

In August, the company launched Muse Code , its own coding agent.

Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users.

The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook , the viral agent platform that made headlines.

articles.title: Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI agent & application、Startup & business
articles.summary: AI agents won't be stealing Uber's lunch any time soon. Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning. The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording "around 500" during […]
articles.full_text:
Transportation AI News Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter Despite growing concerns over AI disintermediation, Uber executives revealed that third-party bots accounted for just four rides and 500 food deliveries out of 320 million transactions.﻿ Despite growing concerns over AI disintermediation, Uber executives revealed that third-party bots accounted for just four rides and 500 food deliveries out of 320 million transactions.﻿ by Andrew J.

Hawkins Nov 4, 2026, 3:58 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Part Of Fall 2026 earnings watch see all Andrew J.

Hawkins is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation.

His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

AI agents won’t be stealing Uber’s lunch any time soon.

Only four rides were arranged by third-party AI agents during the third quarter of 2026, Uber executives disclosed during an earnings call this morning.

The volume of Uber Eats orders fulfilled by AI agents was a little higher, with the company recording “around 500” during the week of Halloween, out of a total 320 million Uber rides and Uber Eats deliveries.

This is the first time that Uber has disclosed the number of third-party AI agents that have arranged deliveries or rides on its platform.

With the rise of AI agents like Meta’s Muse or OpenAI’s Dots, some experts are predicting that platforms like Uber and DoorDash are at risk of disintermediation, in which customers use AI agents to order food or book a ride, rather than visiting the app itself.

But in these early days, it seems like the risk is still very small.

During the call, Uber’s executives expressed an openness to working with third-party AI companies to make things easier for agents to use their platform — while also expressing confidence that their customers will continue to prefer the experience of using the Uber app directly.

Related The DoorDash problem and the great AI browser fight AI could upend food delivery “We hope that there will be more traction,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the call. “We do think that we want to make services that are available to consumers in a delightful, easy way.

We think our direct services are going to be the most delightful and easy, but we will work with these third parties.” He continued, “It is just very, very early, and we want to make sure we are not dependent on any one player, and I think we are very well positioned in this environment going forward.” As we’ve noted before , this first wave of AI agents still have a long way to go before people begin seeing them as a viable way to order food or book a ride somewhere.

There still is a lot of friction points.

And platform operators like Uber or DoorDash have little incentive to allow these agents to barge in and replace their own customers.

Which is not to say the AI companies won’t inevitably figure it out!

These companies know this is one of their primary use cases, and their best path to a more profitable future.

But getting Uber to agree to more disintermediation will be a tough ask.

Uber is developing its own AI tools that are designed to keep customers using its own platform.

Earlier this year, the company rolled out a new Cart Assistant for Uber Eats , in which an AI bot will build a grocery list based on an image of a recipe or a text prompt.

articles.title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
articles.summary: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane wants AI to define the 2028 election, proposing a new social contract that could benefit Americans while also advancing the AI giant’s own business interests.
articles.full_text:
OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI.

And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers .  In a new essay , Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D.

Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order.

He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits.

He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.

The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living.

Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.

Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow.

The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power.

It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.  “Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit.

It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”  While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms.

And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.

Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living.

AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.

Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated.

Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.

Take his proposals for the tax code.

He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing.

Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers. “I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.” Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.

Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers.

He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate.

He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.

Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors.

He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms , arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.

Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.  Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures.

In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities.

Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation , arguing that states could undermine American innovation.

The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.

Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines.

But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.

Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity.

But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI.

Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.

TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

articles.full_text:
Tech AI Google Gemini for Home now plugs into AT&T’s smart security system AT&T’s Connected Life system now supports Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events and more.

AT&T’s Connected Life system now supports Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events and more. by Emma Roth Nov 4, 2026, 8:23 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: AT&T Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

AT&T’s smart home security system now integrates with Gemini for Home.

The company says its Connected Life system is the “first” home security product to integrate with Google Home Premium, enabling a bunch of Gemini-powered features that can summarize home events, search your video history, and more.

With the update, Gemini for Home can provide detailed descriptions about events captured by your security cameras, such as who delivered a package and how many items they dropped off.

You can also search recorded video footage using natural language questions, like “What dug up the yard last night?” or “Who let the dogs out?”, as well as review daily summaries of activity in and outside your home.

These features are only available with AT&T’s professional $29.99 / month Connected Life monitoring plan.

AT&T is also adding the ability to automatically arm or disarm your home based on your proximity to your home.

Related Gemini for Google Home can now use your cameras to trigger automations Google Home’s Gemini AI can handle more complicated requests AT&T launched its Connected Life system last December in partnership with Google and Abode.

It’s now taking advantage of Google’s Gemini-powered Home APIs , which allow smart home brands and developers to build AI-powered features into their devices.

ADT has also hinted at bringing Gemini for Home features into its security systems.

articles.title: DuckDuckGo pitches itself to schools amid backlash over Google’s AI policy
articles.summary: DuckDuckGo is courting schools frustrated by Google's AI restrictions, pointing educators to its search engine and options to disable AI features.
articles.full_text:
DuckDuckGo is pitching itself to schools after Google created an opening for the alternative search engine.

On Tuesday, Google told schools they could turn off Gemini , but it said shutting off its other AI features would cost schools Google Search , as well.

DuckDuckGo, a company that focuses on user privacy by limiting data collection, clearly sees this as a moment to make inroads in education, where Google has historically dominated.

According to figures Google has published in previous years, there are around 50 million Chromebooks in schools, used by students and educators, and its Google Classroom platform serves over 150 million users globally.

On X , DuckDuckGo’s founder and CEO, Gabriel Weinberg, pointed to the company’s online documentation , explaining how schools can switch their default search engine to DuckDuckGo’s service instead, adding, “get in touch for help.” Meanwhile, DuckDuckGo’s chief public affairs officer, Kamyl Bazbaz, issued a stronger statement, writing , “Forcing AI on school children: how a monopolist behaves when they think people are powerless.

Prove Google wrong.” In an email to TechCrunch, DuckDuckGo chastised Google for its decision, adding that Google could easily turn off Search’s AI features for schools if it wanted to.

The company’s comments come as the American public is weighing how much AI they want to allow into their lives.

As Tuesday night’s elections indicate, they don’t want AI data centers built in their towns.

But using AI at work and school has become a common practice and requires a more nuanced discussion.

Knowing that educators have struggled with AI, Google developed technology called “ Guided Learning ” that is meant to help kids learn by walking through problem-solving steps rather than just providing them with an answer.

But educators are still asking for tools that let them remove AI from the learning process altogether.

After the backlash on Tuesday, Google defended its decision, saying it was just responding to schools’ feedback.

It said that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search would be off by default, and schools could choose to enable them individually.

The problem, of course, is that Google Search now heavily uses AI, through AI Overviews and a conversational AI Mode that answers users’ queries.

DuckDuckGo isn’t anti-AI, to be clear — it offers its own set of AI features, including a chat interface called Duck.ai and an AI search assistant.

However, unlike Google, it provides options to disable these features in both its search and browser settings, the company says.

It also offers a dedicated website, noai.duckduckgo.com , where AI-assisted answers, AI-generated images, and AI feature suggestions are all turned off.

That flexibility may be driving demand for its services, as the company reported earlier this year that its app installs were up 30% as users rejected being force-fed Google’s AI Search.
